agent_notes: The subject of שמו is disputed: Moses and Aaron (Metzudat David) or God (Ibn Ezra: 'signs' return to the name; BBE 'he let'). The last word is written דברו (singular) and read דבריו (plural), so the packet shows a Qere; Radak says the sense is the same, general versus particular. I glossed it as 'his word'. Subject of 'rebelled not' is disputed: Moses and Aaron, or the plagues themselves (Rashi, Metzudat David, Meiri). I kept the literal 'they' and mention both readings in the commentary. Psalm 105 places darkness first and out of Exodus order; Ibn Ezra and Malbim offer reasons, which I cite but do not adjudicate.

STEPBible glosses hithallelu as 'boast'. I kept 'boast' in the literal layer, since the Hithpael of hll is reflexive ('make yourselves praised/boast'), and used 'take pride' in the dramatic layer. The five English versions split between 'glory' and 'boast'.

ערב and כנים: STEPBible gives 'swarm of flies' for ערב; the word itself means 'swarm (of mixed creatures)', and whether flies, beetles or wild animals is uncertain. The five English versions split (divers sorts of flies, beetle, dog-fly). I chose 'swarm' in the literal layer and 'flies' in the dramatic one. כנים as 'gnats' follows STEPBible; KJV and ASV 'lice' is the traditional rendering, and the identification is not certain.
בארצם: STEPBible gives 'in their land' with an implied 'was'. I rendered אש להבות as 'fire of flames', keeping the construct, and put the English copula in brackets.

agent_notes: STEPBible and the KJV family render כושל as 'feeble'; the participle is literally 'one stumbling'. I kept 'stumbling' in the literal layer and 'weak' only in the dramatic one. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as 'poor', Radak as 'poor and weak'; Metzudat David reads it as 'stumbling in sin', which I did not follow.

'The dread of them fell upon them' is ambiguous: the first 'them' is Israel, the second Egypt. Metzudat David resolves it that way and Ibn Ezra and Meiri tie it to 'we are all dying' (Ex 12:33). I kept the Hebrew's ambiguity in the literal layer and resolved it only in the dramatic layer and the commentary.
Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion disagree on whether מסך is a canopy overhead or a curtain ahead. I let the commentary state both and chose 'a covering' for the literal layer, which carries both.
ve'uzo is glossed 'and his strength'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'uz as the ark; I give that as one reading and do not adopt it. Neither the Hebrew nor the context forces it.

שָׁאַל has no stated subject. The commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David) all supply Israel. The KJV family follows with 'the people'; I put the supplied subject in brackets in the literal layer. Also the verb is singular, which fits 'Israel' as a collective.

Rashi reads the water as flowing from the well ('the well' as in Num 21), Radak and Malbim place the event at Rephidim. I mention Rephidim as the commentators' identification, not as part of the Hebrew text. Meiri's report of a midrashic reading of ציות as 'ships' (צי) is quoted as his own claim, which I did not verify elsewhere.

עמל is 'toil' and, by metonymy, what toil produces. The KJV 'labour of the people' is literal; I kept 'toil' in the literal layer and explained the metonymy in the commentary. Ibn Ezra's 'houses, olive groves, vineyards' is quoted from the packet only.

The word-gloss for יָהּ follows STEPBible (Yahweh); the literal layer keeps 'Yah' as the short form of the divine name, since the verse's own Hebrew is the abbreviated form, and the dramatic layer uses 'the LORD'.

notes.note: [verse.en:PS.105.3] STEPBible glosses hithallelu as 'boast'. I kept 'boast' in the literal layer, since the Hithpael of hll is reflexive ('make yourselves praised/boast'), and used 'take pride' in the dramatic layer. The five English versions split between 'glory' and 'boast'.
[verse.en:PS.105.4] ve'uzo is glossed 'and his strength'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'uz as the ark; I give that as one reading and do not adopt it. Neither the Hebrew nor the context forces it.
[verse.en:PS.105.8] Meiri's report of the rabbinic reading 'aluf (chief) of the generation' for 'elef dor' is cited, but the literal layer keeps 'a thousand generations'.
[verse.en:PS.105.9] Meiri says the spelling 'Yishchaq' (with sin) is unusual. The same spelling occurs at Amos 7:9 and 7:16 and Jer 33:26; I note the oddity, but I give no explanation for it.

[verse.en:PS.105.11] The shift in this verse from 'to you' (singular, the patriarch addressed) to 'your inheritance' (plural) is kept in the literal layer. It does not appear in the KJV's wording, which keeps 'thee' and 'your', but nothing in the KJV marks it as a shift.
